claims.text: A controlled Ti addition to a W–Cu precursor forms Ti-rich interdendritic regions.
Molten-Cu liquid-metal dealloying selectively removes Ti-rich interdendritic channels from the Ti-doped W–Cu precursor.
The Ti-rich interdendritic regions are lower-melting than the retained phases.
Removing the Ti-rich channels reorganizes Cu into an aligned, interconnected network.
Liquid-metal dealloying of the Ti-doped W–Cu precursor produces an aligned RHEA–Cu microstructure.
The aligned RHEA–Cu microstructure contains continuous Cu pathways.
Continuous, aligned Cu pathways facilitate more efficient heat transfer.
The dealloying treatment retains a robust tungsten framework.
The retained high-melting W phase and resulting RHEA structure maintain mechanical strength.
The retained high-melting W phase and resulting RHEA structure maintain irradiation resistance.
Relative to a conventionally processed W–Cu composite, the dealloyed composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to a conventionally processed W–Cu composite, the dealloyed composite will have no significant decrease in mechanical durability.
Relative to a conventionally processed W–Cu composite, the dealloyed composite will have no significant decrease in irradiation resistance.
The proposed selective dealloying can occur at high temperature in contact with molten Cu without disrupting the tungsten matrix.
Insufficient Ti content may prevent formation of effective sacrificial channels.
Inadequate dealloying temperature or time may cause incomplete dealloying.
Excessive phase removal during dealloying may impair mechanical integrity.
